Whatever He does not will never occurs, just as whatever He wills necessarily occurs.

However, there is a matter here that must be pointed out. God's will, may He be exalted, sometimes relates to His own act and sometimes relates to the act of the servant. Its relation to His own act is that He wills from Himself to assist His servant, grant him success, and prepare him for the act. This will necessitates the servant's act and his will. The will of God for His servant's will alone does not suffice for the occurrence of the act unless He also wills the act itself. For He may will from His servant the will alone, so the servant wills the act and desires it, but does not perform it, because God did not will from Himself to assist him in it and grant him success in it.

This is indicated by His saying, ﴿And you do not will except that God, Lord of the worlds, wills﴾ and His saying, ﴿And they do not remember except that God wills﴾.

These two verses contain the affirmation of the law, the divine decree, the causes and their effects, the act of the servant, and its ascription to the act of the Lord. Each of them has a particular servanthood. The servanthood of the first verse is striving, exhausting one's capacity, free choice, and effort. The servanthood of the second is seeking help from God, relying upon Him, turning to Him, seeking success and aid from Him, and knowing that the servant cannot will or act until God makes him so.

His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ encompasses all of this and contains it. Whoever nullifies either of the two matters has denied the perfection of Lordship (*rubūbiyya*) and nullified it. And success is from God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 81, verses 15–21 (part 1 of 2):

God, glory be to Him, praised His servant Jibril (Gabriel) in the Qur'an in the finest manner, and described him with the most beautiful attributes, saying:
﴿So I swear by the receding stars, (15) the stars that run and hide, (16) and by the night when it retreats, (17) and by the dawn when it breathes, (18) that this is the word of a noble messenger, (19) possessing power, with standing before the Lord of the Throne, (20) obeyed there and trustworthy. (21)﴾
This is Jibril. He described him as God's messenger, as noble in God's sight, as possessing power and a high rank with his Lord, glory be to Him, as obeyed in the heavens, and as trustworthy with the revelation.

As for his nobility before his Lord, he is the closest of the angels to Him.
Some of the early generations (salaf) said: his station with his Lord is like the station of the chamberlain with the king.

As for his power, he lifted up the cities of the people of Lot on his wing, then overturned them upon them.
He is strong in carrying out what he is commanded, unable to fail in it, since the angels of the heavens obey him in what he commands them on behalf of God, exalted is He.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said in his tafsir (exegesis), on the authority of Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Salih: "trustworthy in that he enters seventy pavilions of light without permission."

Describing him as trustworthy requires his truthfulness, his sincerity, and his conveying to the messengers what he was commanded, without addition, subtraction, or concealment.

So the verse combines station, trustworthiness, power, and nearness to God.

A parallel to the combining of station and trustworthiness in him is the words of the Governor to Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us, established and trusted.﴾ [Yusuf: 54]
The combining of power and trustworthiness is like the words of the daughter of Shu'ayb about Musa, peace be upon them both: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy.﴾ [al-Qasas: 26]

(Section)
He said in al-Tibyan:
Among this is God's saying, glory be to Him: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the stars that run and hide﴾
He swore by the stars in their three states: their rising, their running, and their setting.
This is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and the majority of exegetes, and it is the correct one.

Al-khunus is the plural of khanis, and khunus means withdrawing and hiding. From it the devil is called khannas, because he withdraws and shrinks when the servant remembers his Lord. From it is the saying of Abu Hurayrah: "So he withdrew (fa-nkhanasa)." Al-kunus is the plural of kanis, meaning one who enters its kunas, that is, its lair or home. From it: the woman "tkannasat" when she entered her litter, and from it: "the gazelles kanasat" when they took refuge in their lairs.

Al-jawari means the plural of jariyah, like ghashiyah and ghawash. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: "The stars withdraw by day and appear by night." This is also the view of Muqatil, Ata', Qatadah, and others, who said: the planets hide by day, so they are concealed and not seen, and they disappear at the time of their setting. The meaning of "they withdraw" in this view is that they recede from sight and are hidden from it by the daylight covering them. There is another view, that their khunus is their return, and this is their eastward motion, for they have two motions: a motion caused by their own action and a motion by their own nature. Their khunus is their backward motion by their own nature. On this view, the oath is by a type of star, namely the wandering stars (planets).
This is the view of al-Farra'.
There is a third view, that their khunus and kunus is their hiding at the time of their setting, so they set in the places where they set.
This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Since the stars have a state of appearing, a state of hiding, a state of running, and a state of setting, God, glory be to Him, swore by them in all their states. By mentioning their khunus He indicated their state of appearing, because khunus is hiding after appearing, and one does not say of what is still hidden that it has withdrawn. He explicitly mentioned their running and their setting, and their khunus and their appearing. He was content with mentioning their rising by their running, whose beginning is the rising, for rising is the first of their running.
Thus the oath includes their rising, their setting, their running, their hiding, and that is among His signs and proofs of His lordship.

The view of those who explained them as gazelles and wild cattle is not apparent, for several reasons:
First, these states in the wandering stars are a greater sign and lesson.
Second, the people of the earth share in knowing them through observation and sight.
Third, cattle and gazelles have no state in which they are hidden from sight entirely; rather, they are always visible in the open plains.
Fourth, those who explained the verse this way said that their khunus is not from hiding.
Al-Wahidi said: it is from khans in the nose, which is the recession of the nose-tip and the shortness of the bridge; cattle and gazelles have recessed noses, a cow is khansa', and a gazelle is akhnas.
From this the name al-Khansa' derives, from the recession of her nose. It is known that this is a hidden matter that requires reflection, and most people do not know it, whereas the signs of the Lord by which He swears are only apparent and clear, shared in knowledge by all creatures.
The recession in the nose of a cow or gazelle is no greater than the evenness and balance of the nose of the son of Adam, so the sign in the latter is more evident.
Fifth, their kunus in their lairs is no greater than the entry of birds and all other animals into their homes where they shelter, nor is it more evident, so as to be singled out for the oath.
Sixth, if it were the plural of gazelle, it would be said "khans" with a sukun, since it is the plural of akhnas, so it is like ahmar and humr. If it were meant as the plural of a khansa' cow, it would also be on the pattern fa'la', like hamra' and humr. But since its plural came on the pattern fu'al with doubling, it is impossible for it to be the plural of one of the gazelles or cattle, and it is necessarily the plural of khanis, like shahid and shuhud, sa'im and sawm, qa'im and qawm, and their like.
Seventh, it is not clearly acceptable for the Lord, exalted is He, to swear by cattle and gazelles, and this is not the usage or custom of the Qur'an. Rather, God, glory be to Him, swears by the best of each kind, just as when He swore by souls, He swore by the best of them, which is the human soul.
When He swore by His speech, He swore by its noblest and greatest, which is the Qur'an. When He swore by the heavenly things, He swore by the best of them, which are the sky and its sun, moon, and stars.
When He swore by time, He swore by its noblest, which is the ten nights. When He wanted to swear by other than these, He included it in a general term, as in His saying: ﴿So I swear by what you see and what you do not see﴾ and His saying: ﴿the male and the female﴾ in the recitation of the Messenger of God, and similar cases.
Eighth, the conjunction of the oath with the night and the dawn indicates that they are the stars; otherwise it would not be fitting to conjoin cattle and gazelles with night and dawn in one oath.
Abu Ishaq based his argument on this, that they are the stars, saying: this is more fitting to the mention of the stars than to the mention of wild animals.
Ninth, if God had intended that, He would have clarified it and mentioned what indicates it, just as when He intended by the "jawari" the ships, He said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains.﴾
But here there is nothing in the wording or the context indicating that they are cattle and gazelles, while there is in it what indicates that they are the stars, for the reasons we have mentioned and others.
Tenth, the connection between the stars, which are guidance for the travelers and missiles against the devils, and the thing sworn to, which is the Qur'an, which is guidance for the worlds, an adornment for hearts, and a refutation of the devil's doubts, is greater than the connection between cattle, gazelles, and the Qur'an. And God knows best.

(Section)
There is disagreement over the "'as'asa" (approach or departure) of the night: is it its coming or its going? Most scholars hold that 'as'asa means it turned away and departed. This is the view of Ali and Ibn Abbas and his companions.
Al-Hasan said: it came with its darkness, which is one of the two reports from Mujahid.
Whoever favors the coming said: God swore by the coming of the night and the coming of the day, so His saying ﴿and the dawn when it breathes﴾ corresponds to ﴿the night when it retreats﴾.
They said: for this reason God swore by ﴿the night when it covers and the day when it appears﴾ and by the forenoon.
They said: the covering of the night is like its retreat, and the appearing of the day is like the breathing of the dawn, since it is its beginning and its first part.
Whoever favors that it is its departure relies on His saying: ﴿No indeed! By the moon, and by the night when it turns its back, and by the dawn when it brightens﴾, so He swore by the night's departure and the dawn's brightening, which is like the night's retreat and the dawn's breathing.
They said: the better view is that the oath is by the ending of the night and the coming of the day, since it follows it without interval. This is greater in indication and lesson, unlike the coming of the night and the coming of the day, for the oath is not known in the Qur'an by these two. Moreover, there is a long time between them, so the sign in the ending of the one and the arrival of the other immediately after it, without interval, is more eloquent.
So He mentioned the state of this one's weakness and departure, and the state of the other's strength and breathing and approach, which drives away the darkness of the night by its breath. Whenever it breathes, the night flees and turns its back before it. This is the view, and God knows best.

(Section)
Then God, glory be to Him, mentioned the thing sworn to, which is the Qur'an, and informed that it is the word of a noble messenger. Here it is Jibril with certainty, because He described him afterward with what identifies him. As for the noble messenger in al-Haqqah, he is Muhammad, because after it He denied that it is the word of one whom his enemies claimed to be its author. He said: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect.﴾
So He attributed it to the angelic messenger at one time, and to the human messenger at another time. His attribution to each of the two messengers is an attribution of conveying, not of originating it from himself.
Otherwise the two attributions would contradict one another. The word "messenger" indicates this, for the messenger is one who conveys the speech of the one who sent him. This is explicit that it is the speech of the One who sent Jibril and Muhammad, and that each of them conveyed it from God. So it is his word as conveyer, and the word of God, which He spoke truly. There is no ease for one who denies that God speaks the Qur'an, which is His speech in truth, in these two verses. Indeed they are among the clearest proofs that it is the speech of the Lord, exalted is He, and that the two noble messengers have nothing of it except conveying. Jibril heard it from God, and Muhammad heard it from Jibril.

He described his angelic messenger in this surah as noble, strong, established, obeyed in the heavens, and trustworthy with God, the Lord of the Throne. These are five attributes that include the affirmation of the chain of the Qur'an: that it is Muhammad's hearing from Jibril, and Jibril's hearing from the Lord of the worlds. How sublime and exalted is this chain, with God Himself, glory be to Him, attesting to it.

The first attribute: the messenger who brought it to Muhammad is noble, not as his enemies say, that the one who brought it is a devil. The devil is wicked, corrupt, base, ugly in appearance, devoid of good; his inside is worse than his outside, and his outside more hideous than his inside, and there is no good in him or with him. He is the furthest thing from nobility. But the messenger who delivered the Qur'an to Muhammad is noble, beautiful in appearance, radiant in form, abundant in good, pure and purifying, the teacher of the pure. Every good on earth, of guidance, knowledge, recognition, faith, and righteousness, is among what his Lord caused to flow through his hands. This is the utmost in outward and inward nobility.

The second attribute: he possesses power, as He said in another place: ﴿taught by one mighty in power﴾.
In that there are several points of guidance:
First, by his power he prevents the devils from drawing near him, from gaining anything from him, from adding to it or subtracting from it. Rather, when the devil sees him, he flees from him and does not approach him.
Second, he is an ally of this Messenger whom you denied, supporting him, aiding him, and his helper, as God said: ﴿And if you two back each other against him, then indeed God is his protector, and Jibril, and the righteous believers, and the angels after that are a supporting company.﴾
Whoever has this powerful one as his ally, helper, and teacher is the guided and victorious one, and God is his guide and helper.
Third, whoever opposes this Messenger has opposed his companion and ally Jibril, and whoever opposes one who is powerful and mighty is exposed to ruin.
Fourth, he is able to carry out what he is commanded by his power, so he does not fail in that, and the one who delivers it as he was commanded does so by his trustworthiness. Thus he is the strong and trustworthy. When any one of you appoints another for a matter of affairs, whether for a mission, a governorship, an agency, or other, he appoints for it only one who is strong in it and trustworthy in its execution, even if the matter is of the highest importance to him. He appoints one strong, trustworthy, respected, of high standing with him, obeyed among the people, just as God described His servant Jibril with these attributes. This indicates the greatness of the matter of the sender, the messenger, the message, and the one to whom it is sent, since the Noble, the Strong, the Established with Him, the Obeyed in the Exalted Assembly, the Trustworthy in the truest sense, was appointed for it. Kings do not send in their important matters except the nobles of high rank and lofty status.

His saying ﴿possessing power, with standing before the Lord of the Throne﴾ means: he has standing and eminence with Him, and he is the closest of the angels to Him.
In His saying ﴿before the Lord of the Throne﴾ there is an indication of the elevation of Jibril's rank, since he is near the Lord of the Throne, glory be to Him.
In His saying ﴿obeyed there﴾ there is an indication that his hosts and helpers obey him when he dispatches them to support his companion and beloved Muhammad. There is also an indication that this one you deny and oppose will become obeyed on earth just as Jibril is obeyed in the heavens, and that each of the two messengers is obeyed in his place and among his people.
There is also in it an honoring of him, for he is in the position of obeyed kings among their people, so no one was appointed for this great matter except such an obeyed king.
In describing him as trustworthy there is an indication of his guarding what he was entrusted with and his delivering it as it should be.

Then He exonerated and purified His human messenger from what his enemies say about him, saying: ﴿And your companion is not mad.﴾
This is something they know and do not doubt, even though they say otherwise with their tongues; they know that they were liars.

Then He informed of his seeing Jibril. This implies that he is an angel existing in external reality, seen with the eyes and perceived by sight, not as the philosophers and their followers claim, that he is the "active intellect" and not something perceived by sight. Their reality, according to them, is an imagined form existing in minds, not in external reality. This is among the things by which they departed from all the messengers and their followers, and by which they left all the religions. For this reason, establishing the Prophet's seeing of Jibril is more important than establishing his seeing of his Lord, exalted is He. His seeing of Jibril is the foundation of faith, which is not complete except by believing it, and whoever denies it disbelieves with certainty. As for his seeing of his Lord, exalted is He, its best case is that it is a matter of dispute, whose denier does not become a disbeliever by consensus. A group of the Companions explicitly stated that he did not see Him, and Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi related the consensus of the Companions on that. So we are more in need of establishing his seeing of Jibril than of establishing his seeing of his Lord, exalted is He, even though the seeing of the Lord is greater than the seeing of Jibril and those below him, for prophethood is not at all dependent on it.

Then He exonerated both of His messengers, one by way of explicit statement and the other by way of implication, from what contradicts the purpose of the message: concealment, which is stinginess and miserliness, and alteration and change, which bring suspicion. So He said: ﴿And he is not stingy regarding the unseen.﴾
For the purpose of the message is not fulfilled except by two things: delivering it without concealment, and delivering it as it is, without addition or subtraction. The two readings are like the two verses. One of them, the reading with the letter dad, exonerates him from stinginess, for the dhanin is the miser. One says "dhanantu bihi, adhannu" like "bakhiltu bihi, abkhalu," with the same meaning. From it is the saying of Jamil ibn Ma'mar:
"I give generously of my cherished inheritance, but I am stingy with your secret toward whoever asks me."

Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: he is not stingy with what God sent down. Mujahid said: he does not withhold from them what he knows.
The exegetes agreed that the unseen here means the Qur'an and the revelation.
Al-Farra' said: God says, "The unseen of the heavens comes to him," and it is breathed into him, so he is not stingy with it toward you. This is a very good meaning, for the nature of souls is to be stingy with a precious thing, especially toward one who does not know its worth and disparages it and those in whose possession it is. Yet this messenger does not withhold from you the revelation, which is the most precious and greatest of things.
Abu Ali al-Farisi said: the meaning is that the unseen comes to him, and he clarifies it, informs of it, and makes it manifest, and does not conceal it, as the soothsayer conceals what he has and hides it until he takes a bribe for it. There is also another meaning in it: that he is certain of the unseen he informs of, so he does not fear that it will be refuted and the matter will appear contrary to what he informed. This is unlike soothsayers and others who inform of the unseen, for their lies outnumber their truths. And when one of them informs of a report, he is not certain of it, but rather fears the exposure of his lie. So this Messenger's proceeding to inform of this great unseen, which is the greatest of the unseen, confident in it, steadfast in it, displaying it in every assembly, repeating and proclaiming it, and challenging his enemies with it, is among the greatest proofs of his truthfulness.

As for the reading of one who read "bi-dhanin" with the letter zha', its meaning is "accused," from "zanantu Zaydan," meaning "I accused Zayd." It is not from the zann that means perception and apprehension, for that transitive verb takes two objects. From it is what Abu Ubaydah recited:
"By the Book of God, I did not abandon you out of hatred, but the lover is one who is suspected."
The meaning is: this Messenger is not one accused regarding the Qur'an; rather he is trustworthy, adding nothing to it and subtracting nothing from it.

This indicates that the pronoun refers to Muhammad, since the angelic messenger's trustworthiness was already described, and then He said: ﴿And your companion is not mad,﴾ and then He said: "And he is not," i.e., your companion is neither accused nor stingy.

Abu Ubaydah preferred the reading with the letter zha' for two reasons:

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 81, verses 15–21 (part 2 of 2)**

The first point is that the disbelievers did not accuse him of stinginess (*bukhl*). They accused him of falsehood, so negating the accusation is more appropriate than negating stinginess.

The second point is that He said *ʿala al-ghayb* ("concerning the unseen"). Had He meant stinginess, He would have said *bi al-ghayb*, because one says "so-and-so is stingy with such-and-such" (*fulan ḍanīn bi-kadhā*), and it is rarely said "stingy concerning such-and-such" (*ʿalā kadhā*).

I say: What supports this is that He described him with the same quality by which He described His messenger the angel, namely trustworthiness (*amāna*). So He negated the accusation against him, just as He described Gabriel as "trustworthy." What also supports it is that He negated every kind of lying from what he brought of the unseen. For if it were a lie, it would have come either from him or from one who taught him. If it came from the one who taught him, then he is not an accursed devil. If it came from him with deliberate intent, then he is the accused, the opposite of the trustworthy. If it came from him without intent, then he is a madman. So God negated all of that from His messenger and vouched for the authenticity of the Qur'an in the highest possible way.

For this reason He said, ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾. It is not the teaching of Satan, nor is Satan able to do it, nor is it befitting for him. As He said, ﴿The devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able to do it﴾. He negated their action, their seeking it, and their capacity for it. Anyone with even minimal knowledge of the conditions of devils, madmen, and the accused, and of the conditions of the messengers, knows with certainty, beyond any dispute or doubt, a knowledge as necessary as other necessary truths, that the two are mutually exclusive and opposed, like two contraries that cannot coexist. Indeed, the incompatibility between the two matters is more evident to reason than the incompatibility between light and darkness is to sight. For this reason God rebuked those who disbelieved after this clear distinction between the call of the messengers and the call of the devils became apparent, saying, ﴿Where then are you going?﴾

Abu Ishaq said: "Which path could you take that is clearer than this path that has been made clear to you?"

I say: This is among the finest and clearest forms of argument: that you make the listener understand the truth, and then say to him, "What would you say to the contrary of this, and where would you go in opposition to it?" God said, ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ and ﴿Then in what statement after God and His signs will they believe?﴾ So the matter is confined to truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance. When you turn away from guidance and truth, then where is the turning, and where is the path?

A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Then would you, if you turned away, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ That is, if you turn away from belief in the Qur'an and the messenger and from obeying him, then there remains nothing but corruption on earth, polytheism, sins, and severing of kinship. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Rather, they have denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state﴾. When they abandoned the truth and turned away from it, their affair became confused for them, and they became perplexed, not knowing what to say or what to do. Indeed, they say nothing without it being false, and they do nothing without it being wasted and profitless for them. This is the condition of everyone who departs from the path that leads to the goal. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿So if they do not respond to you, know that they only follow their own desires﴾. This meaning has been fully disclosed by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿Such is God, your true Lord. So what is there after the truth but error? How then are you turned away?﴾

**(Section)**

Then God informed us about the Qur'an that it is (a reminder to the worlds), and in another place (a reminder to the God-fearing), and in another place it is for His messenger and his people, and in another place it is a reminder in general terms, and in another place it is a blessed reminder, and in another place He described it as "possessing the reminder" (*dhū al-dhikr*).

By gathering these passages, the meaning of its being a reminder in both general and specific senses, and of its being "possessing the reminder," becomes clear. It reminds the servants of their welfare in this life and the next. It reminds them of the origin and the return. It reminds them of the Lord, may He be exalted, of His names, attributes, and actions, and of His rights over His servants. It reminds them of good, so that they may seek it, and of evil, so that they may avoid it. It reminds them of their own souls, their states, their afflictions, and what perfects them. It reminds them of their enemy, of what he desires from them, of what they should guard against of his plots, and from which doors and paths he comes to them. It reminds them of their poverty and their need for Him, and that they are compelled to Him and cannot dispense with Him for a single moment. It reminds them of His blessings upon them, and calls them through these blessings to greater blessings. It reminds them of His might, the severity of His seizing, and His vengeance upon those who disobey His command and deny His messengers. It reminds them of His reward and His punishment.

For this reason God commands His servants to remember what is in His Book, as He said, ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with strength and remember what is in it, that you may become righteous."﴾

Since this is so, the most worthy, the most fitting, and the first to be a remembrancer of it is the one to whom it was revealed, then his people, then all the worlds. As for why it is specifically given to the God-fearing, it is because they are the ones who benefit from its reminder.

As for describing it as "possessing the reminder," it is because it contains the reminder. So it is the possessor of the reminder, the reminder comes from it, and the reminder is in it, just as it is guidance and guidance is in it, healing and healing is in it, and mercy and mercy is in it.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿for whoever among you wills to be upright﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "the worlds." It is a substitute of part for whole (*badal baʿḍ min kull*). This is among the finest proofs that a substitute is equivalent to the mention of two intended governing elements. For the aspect in which it is a reminder to all the worlds is different from the aspect in which it is a reminder to the people of uprightness. It is a reminder to the general public in terms of its suitability and potential, and a reminder to the people of uprightness in terms of actual attainment and benefit. Just as the substitute is more specific than the element it replaces, the implied governing element in it is more specific than the explicit governing element in what it replaces. This must be understood, so consider it carefully.

His saying ﴿for whoever among you wills﴾ is a refutation of the Jabriyya (the determinists, *al-Jabriyya*), who claim that the servant has no will, or that his will is merely a sign of the occurrence of the act, with no real connection between them other than a customary concomitance that is not a cause of it.

His saying ﴿And you do not will except that God wills﴾ is a refutation of the Qadariyya (those who affirm human power, *al-Qadariyya*), who claim that the servant's will is independent in bringing the act into existence, without depending on the will of God. Rather, whenever the servant wills the act, it occurs. According to them, it is impossible for God's will to relate to the servant's act; rather, he does it without God's will.

Thus the two verses refute the claims of both groups.

If the determinist says, "He, may He be exalted, did not say that the act occurs by the servant's will; rather He reported that uprightness is attained when the servant wills. We agree with that." And if the Qadari says, "His saying ﴿And you do not will except that God wills﴾ is to be understood as: the servant's will is what necessitates the act by which it occurs, and God's will for the act is His command to do so. We do not deny that."

The answer is that both groups have distorted the text. As for the determinist, it is said to him: according to you, the concomitance of the act with the servant's will is like its concomitance with his existence, his form, and all his other purposes, which have no influence on the act. For according to you, the relation of all his purposes to the act, in terms of having no influence, is a relation of will, and the concomitance is present with all his purposes. So what made the will specifically distinct, in the innate nature, the minds, or the laws of people, between the relation of will and volition to the act and the relation of all the other purposes of the living being, if according to you it is nothing but a customary concomitance? And customary concomitance is present with all of them.

As for the Qadari, his distortion is more severe, because he interpreted "will" as "command." He said that the meaning is: "You do not will except by God's command." This is decisively false, for "will" in the Qur'an is not used in that sense. It is used in the sense of the will of creative decree (*mashīʾat al-takwīn*), as in His saying, ﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾, and His saying, ﴿Had God willed, they would not have fought one another﴾, and His saying, ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾, and His saying, ﴿Have those who believe not despaired that had God willed, He would have guided all of mankind?﴾ and similar passages in which it is impossible to interpret the will as command in any way.

What the verse indicates, together with the other proofs of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) and the clear proofs of reason, is that the wills of the servants are among the existing things that do not come into being except by the will of God, may He be exalted. Whatever He does not will never occurs, just as whatever He wills necessarily occurs.

However, there is a matter here that must be pointed out. God's will, may He be exalted, sometimes relates to His own act and sometimes relates to the act of the servant. Its relation to His own act is that He wills from Himself to assist His servant, grant him success, and prepare him for the act. This will necessitates the servant's act and his will. The will of God for His servant's will alone does not suffice for the occurrence of the act unless He also wills the act itself. For He may will from His servant the will alone, so the servant wills the act and desires it, but does not perform it, because God did not will from Himself to assist him in it and grant him success in it.

This is indicated by His saying, ﴿And you do not will except that God, Lord of the worlds, wills﴾ and His saying, ﴿And they do not remember except that God wills﴾.

These two verses contain the affirmation of the law, the divine decree, the causes and their effects, the act of the servant, and its ascription to the act of the Lord. Each of them has a particular servanthood. The servanthood of the first verse is striving, exhausting one's capacity, free choice, and effort. The servanthood of the second is seeking help from God, relying upon Him, turning to Him, seeking success and aid from Him, and knowing that the servant cannot will or act until God makes him so.

His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ encompasses all of this and contains it. Whoever nullifies either of the two matters has denied the perfection of Lordship (*rubūbiyya*) and nullified it. And success is from God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 81, verses 15–21 (part 1 of 2):

God, glory be to Him, praised His servant Jibril (Gabriel) in the Qur'an in the finest manner, and described him with the most beautiful attributes, saying:
﴿So I swear by the receding stars, (15) the stars that run and hide, (16) and by the night when it retreats, (17) and by the dawn when it breathes, (18) that this is the word of a noble messenger, (19) possessing power, with standing before the Lord of the Throne, (20) obeyed there and trustworthy. (21)﴾
This is Jibril. He described him as God's messenger, as noble in God's sight, as possessing power and a high rank with his Lord, glory be to Him, as obeyed in the heavens, and as trustworthy with the revelation.

As for his nobility before his Lord, he is the closest of the angels to Him.
Some of the early generations (salaf) said: his station with his Lord is like the station of the chamberlain with the king.

As for his power, he lifted up the cities of the people of Lot on his wing, then overturned them upon them.
He is strong in carrying out what he is commanded, unable to fail in it, since the angels of the heavens obey him in what he commands them on behalf of God, exalted is He.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said in his tafsir (exegesis), on the authority of Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Salih: "trustworthy in that he enters seventy pavilions of light without permission."

Describing him as trustworthy requires his truthfulness, his sincerity, and his conveying to the messengers what he was commanded, without addition, subtraction, or concealment.

So the verse combines station, trustworthiness, power, and nearness to God.

A parallel to the combining of station and trustworthiness in him is the words of the Governor to Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us, established and trusted.﴾ [Yusuf: 54]
The combining of power and trustworthiness is like the words of the daughter of Shu'ayb about Musa, peace be upon them both: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy.﴾ [al-Qasas: 26]

(Section)
He said in al-Tibyan:
Among this is God's saying, glory be to Him: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the stars that run and hide﴾
He swore by the stars in their three states: their rising, their running, and their setting.
This is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and the majority of exegetes, and it is the correct one.

Al-khunus is the plural of khanis, and khunus means withdrawing and hiding. From it the devil is called khannas, because he withdraws and shrinks when the servant remembers his Lord. From it is the saying of Abu Hurayrah: "So he withdrew (fa-nkhanasa)." Al-kunus is the plural of kanis, meaning one who enters its kunas, that is, its lair or home. From it: the woman "tkannasat" when she entered her litter, and from it: "the gazelles kanasat" when they took refuge in their lairs.

Al-jawari means the plural of jariyah, like ghashiyah and ghawash. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: "The stars withdraw by day and appear by night." This is also the view of Muqatil, Ata', Qatadah, and others, who said: the planets hide by day, so they are concealed and not seen, and they disappear at the time of their setting. The meaning of "they withdraw" in this view is that they recede from sight and are hidden from it by the daylight covering them. There is another view, that their khunus is their return, and this is their eastward motion, for they have two motions: a motion caused by their own action and a motion by their own nature. Their khunus is their backward motion by their own nature. On this view, the oath is by a type of star, namely the wandering stars (planets).
This is the view of al-Farra'.
There is a third view, that their khunus and kunus is their hiding at the time of their setting, so they set in the places where they set.
This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Since the stars have a state of appearing, a state of hiding, a state of running, and a state of setting, God, glory be to Him, swore by them in all their states. By mentioning their khunus He indicated their state of appearing, because khunus is hiding after appearing, and one does not say of what is still hidden that it has withdrawn. He explicitly mentioned their running and their setting, and their khunus and their appearing. He was content with mentioning their rising by their running, whose beginning is the rising, for rising is the first of their running.
Thus the oath includes their rising, their setting, their running, their hiding, and that is among His signs and proofs of His lordship.

The view of those who explained them as gazelles and wild cattle is not apparent, for several reasons:
First, these states in the wandering stars are a greater sign and lesson.
Second, the people of the earth share in knowing them through observation and sight.
Third, cattle and gazelles have no state in which they are hidden from sight entirely; rather, they are always visible in the open plains.
Fourth, those who explained the verse this way said that their khunus is not from hiding.
Al-Wahidi said: it is from khans in the nose, which is the recession of the nose-tip and the shortness of the bridge; cattle and gazelles have recessed noses, a cow is khansa', and a gazelle is akhnas.
From this the name al-Khansa' derives, from the recession of her nose. It is known that this is a hidden matter that requires reflection, and most people do not know it, whereas the signs of the Lord by which He swears are only apparent and clear, shared in knowledge by all creatures.
The recession in the nose of a cow or gazelle is no greater than the evenness and balance of the nose of the son of Adam, so the sign in the latter is more evident.
Fifth, their kunus in their lairs is no greater than the entry of birds and all other animals into their homes where they shelter, nor is it more evident, so as to be singled out for the oath.
Sixth, if it were the plural of gazelle, it would be said "khans" with a sukun, since it is the plural of akhnas, so it is like ahmar and humr. If it were meant as the plural of a khansa' cow, it would also be on the pattern fa'la', like hamra' and humr. But since its plural came on the pattern fu'al with doubling, it is impossible for it to be the plural of one of the gazelles or cattle, and it is necessarily the plural of khanis, like shahid and shuhud, sa'im and sawm, qa'im and qawm, and their like.
Seventh, it is not clearly acceptable for the Lord, exalted is He, to swear by cattle and gazelles, and this is not the usage or custom of the Qur'an. Rather, God, glory be to Him, swears by the best of each kind, just as when He swore by souls, He swore by the best of them, which is the human soul.
When He swore by His speech, He swore by its noblest and greatest, which is the Qur'an. When He swore by the heavenly things, He swore by the best of them, which are the sky and its sun, moon, and stars.
When He swore by time, He swore by its noblest, which is the ten nights. When He wanted to swear by other than these, He included it in a general term, as in His saying: ﴿So I swear by what you see and what you do not see﴾ and His saying: ﴿the male and the female﴾ in the recitation of the Messenger of God, and similar cases.
Eighth, the conjunction of the oath with the night and the dawn indicates that they are the stars; otherwise it would not be fitting to conjoin cattle and gazelles with night and dawn in one oath.
Abu Ishaq based his argument on this, that they are the stars, saying: this is more fitting to the mention of the stars than to the mention of wild animals.
Ninth, if God had intended that, He would have clarified it and mentioned what indicates it, just as when He intended by the "jawari" the ships, He said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains.﴾
But here there is nothing in the wording or the context indicating that they are cattle and gazelles, while there is in it what indicates that they are the stars, for the reasons we have mentioned and others.
Tenth, the connection between the stars, which are guidance for the travelers and missiles against the devils, and the thing sworn to, which is the Qur'an, which is guidance for the worlds, an adornment for hearts, and a refutation of the devil's doubts, is greater than the connection between cattle, gazelles, and the Qur'an. And God knows best.

(Section)
There is disagreement over the "'as'asa" (approach or departure) of the night: is it its coming or its going? Most scholars hold that 'as'asa means it turned away and departed. This is the view of Ali and Ibn Abbas and his companions.
Al-Hasan said: it came with its darkness, which is one of the two reports from Mujahid.
Whoever favors the coming said: God swore by the coming of the night and the coming of the day, so His saying ﴿and the dawn when it breathes﴾ corresponds to ﴿the night when it retreats﴾.
They said: for this reason God swore by ﴿the night when it covers and the day when it appears﴾ and by the forenoon.
They said: the covering of the night is like its retreat, and the appearing of the day is like the breathing of the dawn, since it is its beginning and its first part.
Whoever favors that it is its departure relies on His saying: ﴿No indeed! By the moon, and by the night when it turns its back, and by the dawn when it brightens﴾, so He swore by the night's departure and the dawn's brightening, which is like the night's retreat and the dawn's breathing.
They said: the better view is that the oath is by the ending of the night and the coming of the day, since it follows it without interval. This is greater in indication and lesson, unlike the coming of the night and the coming of the day, for the oath is not known in the Qur'an by these two. Moreover, there is a long time between them, so the sign in the ending of the one and the arrival of the other immediately after it, without interval, is more eloquent.
So He mentioned the state of this one's weakness and departure, and the state of the other's strength and breathing and approach, which drives away the darkness of the night by its breath. Whenever it breathes, the night flees and turns its back before it. This is the view, and God knows best.

(Section)
Then God, glory be to Him, mentioned the thing sworn to, which is the Qur'an, and informed that it is the word of a noble messenger. Here it is Jibril with certainty, because He described him afterward with what identifies him. As for the noble messenger in al-Haqqah, he is Muhammad, because after it He denied that it is the word of one whom his enemies claimed to be its author. He said: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect.﴾
So He attributed it to the angelic messenger at one time, and to the human messenger at another time. His attribution to each of the two messengers is an attribution of conveying, not of originating it from himself.
Otherwise the two attributions would contradict one another. The word "messenger" indicates this, for the messenger is one who conveys the speech of the one who sent him. This is explicit that it is the speech of the One who sent Jibril and Muhammad, and that each of them conveyed it from God. So it is his word as conveyer, and the word of God, which He spoke truly. There is no ease for one who denies that God speaks the Qur'an, which is His speech in truth, in these two verses. Indeed they are among the clearest proofs that it is the speech of the Lord, exalted is He, and that the two noble messengers have nothing of it except conveying. Jibril heard it from God, and Muhammad heard it from Jibril.

He described his angelic messenger in this surah as noble, strong, established, obeyed in the heavens, and trustworthy with God, the Lord of the Throne. These are five attributes that include the affirmation of the chain of the Qur'an: that it is Muhammad's hearing from Jibril, and Jibril's hearing from the Lord of the worlds. How sublime and exalted is this chain, with God Himself, glory be to Him, attesting to it.

The first attribute: the messenger who brought it to Muhammad is noble, not as his enemies say, that the one who brought it is a devil. The devil is wicked, corrupt, base, ugly in appearance, devoid of good; his inside is worse than his outside, and his outside more hideous than his inside, and there is no good in him or with him. He is the furthest thing from nobility. But the messenger who delivered the Qur'an to Muhammad is noble, beautiful in appearance, radiant in form, abundant in good, pure and purifying, the teacher of the pure. Every good on earth, of guidance, knowledge, recognition, faith, and righteousness, is among what his Lord caused to flow through his hands. This is the utmost in outward and inward nobility.

The second attribute: he possesses power, as He said in another place: ﴿taught by one mighty in power﴾.
In that there are several points of guidance:
First, by his power he prevents the devils from drawing near him, from gaining anything from him, from adding to it or subtracting from it. Rather, when the devil sees him, he flees from him and does not approach him.
Second, he is an ally of this Messenger whom you denied, supporting him, aiding him, and his helper, as God said: ﴿And if you two back each other against him, then indeed God is his protector, and Jibril, and the righteous believers, and the angels after that are a supporting company.﴾
Whoever has this powerful one as his ally, helper, and teacher is the guided and victorious one, and God is his guide and helper.
Third, whoever opposes this Messenger has opposed his companion and ally Jibril, and whoever opposes one who is powerful and mighty is exposed to ruin.
Fourth, he is able to carry out what he is commanded by his power, so he does not fail in that, and the one who delivers it as he was commanded does so by his trustworthiness. Thus he is the strong and trustworthy. When any one of you appoints another for a matter of affairs, whether for a mission, a governorship, an agency, or other, he appoints for it only one who is strong in it and trustworthy in its execution, even if the matter is of the highest importance to him. He appoints one strong, trustworthy, respected, of high standing with him, obeyed among the people, just as God described His servant Jibril with these attributes. This indicates the greatness of the matter of the sender, the messenger, the message, and the one to whom it is sent, since the Noble, the Strong, the Established with Him, the Obeyed in the Exalted Assembly, the Trustworthy in the truest sense, was appointed for it. Kings do not send in their important matters except the nobles of high rank and lofty status.

His saying ﴿possessing power, with standing before the Lord of the Throne﴾ means: he has standing and eminence with Him, and he is the closest of the angels to Him.
In His saying ﴿before the Lord of the Throne﴾ there is an indication of the elevation of Jibril's rank, since he is near the Lord of the Throne, glory be to Him.
In His saying ﴿obeyed there﴾ there is an indication that his hosts and helpers obey him when he dispatches them to support his companion and beloved Muhammad. There is also an indication that this one you deny and oppose will become obeyed on earth just as Jibril is obeyed in the heavens, and that each of the two messengers is obeyed in his place and among his people.
There is also in it an honoring of him, for he is in the position of obeyed kings among their people, so no one was appointed for this great matter except such an obeyed king.
In describing him as trustworthy there is an indication of his guarding what he was entrusted with and his delivering it as it should be.

Then He exonerated and purified His human messenger from what his enemies say about him, saying: ﴿And your companion is not mad.﴾
This is something they know and do not doubt, even though they say otherwise with their tongues; they know that they were liars.

Then He informed of his seeing Jibril. This implies that he is an angel existing in external reality, seen with the eyes and perceived by sight, not as the philosophers and their followers claim, that he is the "active intellect" and not something perceived by sight. Their reality, according to them, is an imagined form existing in minds, not in external reality. This is among the things by which they departed from all the messengers and their followers, and by which they left all the religions. For this reason, establishing the Prophet's seeing of Jibril is more important than establishing his seeing of his Lord, exalted is He. His seeing of Jibril is the foundation of faith, which is not complete except by believing it, and whoever denies it disbelieves with certainty. As for his seeing of his Lord, exalted is He, its best case is that it is a matter of dispute, whose denier does not become a disbeliever by consensus. A group of the Companions explicitly stated that he did not see Him, and Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi related the consensus of the Companions on that. So we are more in need of establishing his seeing of Jibril than of establishing his seeing of his Lord, exalted is He, even though the seeing of the Lord is greater than the seeing of Jibril and those below him, for prophethood is not at all dependent on it.

Then He exonerated both of His messengers, one by way of explicit statement and the other by way of implication, from what contradicts the purpose of the message: concealment, which is stinginess and miserliness, and alteration and change, which bring suspicion. So He said: ﴿And he is not stingy regarding the unseen.﴾
For the purpose of the message is not fulfilled except by two things: delivering it without concealment, and delivering it as it is, without addition or subtraction. The two readings are like the two verses. One of them, the reading with the letter dad, exonerates him from stinginess, for the dhanin is the miser. One says "dhanantu bihi, adhannu" like "bakhiltu bihi, abkhalu," with the same meaning. From it is the saying of Jamil ibn Ma'mar:
"I give generously of my cherished inheritance, but I am stingy with your secret toward whoever asks me."

Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: he is not stingy with what God sent down. Mujahid said: he does not withhold from them what he knows.
The exegetes agreed that the unseen here means the Qur'an and the revelation.
Al-Farra' said: God says, "The unseen of the heavens comes to him," and it is breathed into him, so he is not stingy with it toward you. This is a very good meaning, for the nature of souls is to be stingy with a precious thing, especially toward one who does not know its worth and disparages it and those in whose possession it is. Yet this messenger does not withhold from you the revelation, which is the most precious and greatest of things.
Abu Ali al-Farisi said: the meaning is that the unseen comes to him, and he clarifies it, informs of it, and makes it manifest, and does not conceal it, as the soothsayer conceals what he has and hides it until he takes a bribe for it. There is also another meaning in it: that he is certain of the unseen he informs of, so he does not fear that it will be refuted and the matter will appear contrary to what he informed. This is unlike soothsayers and others who inform of the unseen, for their lies outnumber their truths. And when one of them informs of a report, he is not certain of it, but rather fears the exposure of his lie. So this Messenger's proceeding to inform of this great unseen, which is the greatest of the unseen, confident in it, steadfast in it, displaying it in every assembly, repeating and proclaiming it, and challenging his enemies with it, is among the greatest proofs of his truthfulness.

As for the reading of one who read "bi-dhanin" with the letter zha', its meaning is "accused," from "zanantu Zaydan," meaning "I accused Zayd." It is not from the zann that means perception and apprehension, for that transitive verb takes two objects. From it is what Abu Ubaydah recited:
"By the Book of God, I did not abandon you out of hatred, but the lover is one who is suspected."
The meaning is: this Messenger is not one accused regarding the Qur'an; rather he is trustworthy, adding nothing to it and subtracting nothing from it.

This indicates that the pronoun refers to Muhammad, since the angelic messenger's trustworthiness was already described, and then He said: ﴿And your companion is not mad,﴾ and then He said: "And he is not," i.e., your companion is neither accused nor stingy.

Abu Ubaydah preferred the reading with the letter zha' for two reasons:

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 81, verses 15–21 (part 2 of 2)**

The first point is that the disbelievers did not accuse him of stinginess (*bukhl*). They accused him of falsehood, so negating the accusation is more appropriate than negating stinginess.

The second point is that He said *ʿala al-ghayb* ("concerning the unseen"). Had He meant stinginess, He would have said *bi al-ghayb*, because one says "so-and-so is stingy with such-and-such" (*fulan ḍanīn bi-kadhā*), and it is rarely said "stingy concerning such-and-such" (*ʿalā kadhā*).

I say: What supports this is that He described him with the same quality by which He described His messenger the angel, namely trustworthiness (*amāna*). So He negated the accusation against him, just as He described Gabriel as "trustworthy." What also supports it is that He negated every kind of lying from what he brought of the unseen. For if it were a lie, it would have come either from him or from one who taught him. If it came from the one who taught him, then he is not an accursed devil. If it came from him with deliberate intent, then he is the accused, the opposite of the trustworthy. If it came from him without intent, then he is a madman. So God negated all of that from His messenger and vouched for the authenticity of the Qur'an in the highest possible way.

For this reason He said, ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾. It is not the teaching of Satan, nor is Satan able to do it, nor is it befitting for him. As He said, ﴿The devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able to do it﴾. He negated their action, their seeking it, and their capacity for it. Anyone with even minimal knowledge of the conditions of devils, madmen, and the accused, and of the conditions of the messengers, knows with certainty, beyond any dispute or doubt, a knowledge as necessary as other necessary truths, that the two are mutually exclusive and opposed, like two contraries that cannot coexist. Indeed, the incompatibility between the two matters is more evident to reason than the incompatibility between light and darkness is to sight. For this reason God rebuked those who disbelieved after this clear distinction between the call of the messengers and the call of the devils became apparent, saying, ﴿Where then are you going?﴾

Abu Ishaq said: "Which path could you take that is clearer than this path that has been made clear to you?"

I say: This is among the finest and clearest forms of argument: that you make the listener understand the truth, and then say to him, "What would you say to the contrary of this, and where would you go in opposition to it?" God said, ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ and ﴿Then in what statement after God and His signs will they believe?﴾ So the matter is confined to truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance. When you turn away from guidance and truth, then where is the turning, and where is the path?

A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Then would you, if you turned away, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ That is, if you turn away from belief in the Qur'an and the messenger and from obeying him, then there remains nothing but corruption on earth, polytheism, sins, and severing of kinship. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Rather, they have denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state﴾. When they abandoned the truth and turned away from it, their affair became confused for them, and they became perplexed, not knowing what to say or what to do. Indeed, they say nothing without it being false, and they do nothing without it being wasted and profitless for them. This is the condition of everyone who departs from the path that leads to the goal. A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿So if they do not respond to you, know that they only follow their own desires﴾. This meaning has been fully disclosed by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿Such is God, your true Lord. So what is there after the truth but error? How then are you turned away?﴾

**(Section)**

Then God informed us about the Qur'an that it is (a reminder to the worlds), and in another place (a reminder to the God-fearing), and in another place it is for His messenger and his people, and in another place it is a reminder in general terms, and in another place it is a blessed reminder, and in another place He described it as "possessing the reminder" (*dhū al-dhikr*).

By gathering these passages, the meaning of its being a reminder in both general and specific senses, and of its being "possessing the reminder," becomes clear. It reminds the servants of their welfare in this life and the next. It reminds them of the origin and the return. It reminds them of the Lord, may He be exalted, of His names, attributes, and actions, and of His rights over His servants. It reminds them of good, so that they may seek it, and of evil, so that they may avoid it. It reminds them of their own souls, their states, their afflictions, and what perfects them. It reminds them of their enemy, of what he desires from them, of what they should guard against of his plots, and from which doors and paths he comes to them. It reminds them of their poverty and their need for Him, and that they are compelled to Him and cannot dispense with Him for a single moment. It reminds them of His blessings upon them, and calls them through these blessings to greater blessings. It reminds them of His might, the severity of His seizing, and His vengeance upon those who disobey His command and deny His messengers. It reminds them of His reward and His punishment.

For this reason God commands His servants to remember what is in His Book, as He said, ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with strength and remember what is in it, that you may become righteous."﴾

Since this is so, the most worthy, the most fitting, and the first to be a remembrancer of it is the one to whom it was revealed, then his people, then all the worlds. As for why it is specifically given to the God-fearing, it is because they are the ones who benefit from its reminder.

As for describing it as "possessing the reminder," it is because it contains the reminder. So it is the possessor of the reminder, the reminder comes from it, and the reminder is in it, just as it is guidance and guidance is in it, healing and healing is in it, and mercy and mercy is in it.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿for whoever among you wills to be upright﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "the worlds." It is a substitute of part for whole (*badal baʿḍ min kull*). This is among the finest proofs that a substitute is equivalent to the mention of two intended governing elements. For the aspect in which it is a reminder to all the worlds is different from the aspect in which it is a reminder to the people of uprightness. It is a reminder to the general public in terms of its suitability and potential, and a reminder to the people of uprightness in terms of actual attainment and benefit. Just as the substitute is more specific than the element it replaces, the implied governing element in it is more specific than the explicit governing element in what it replaces. This must be understood, so consider it carefully.

His saying ﴿for whoever among you wills﴾ is a refutation of the Jabriyya (the determinists, *al-Jabriyya*), who claim that the servant has no will, or that his will is merely a sign of the occurrence of the act, with no real connection between them other than a customary concomitance that is not a cause of it.

His saying ﴿And you do not will except that God wills﴾ is a refutation of the Qadariyya (those who affirm human power, *al-Qadariyya*), who claim that the servant's will is independent in bringing the act into existence, without depending on the will of God. Rather, whenever the servant wills the act, it occurs. According to them, it is impossible for God's will to relate to the servant's act; rather, he does it without God's will.

Thus the two verses refute the claims of both groups.

If the determinist says, "He, may He be exalted, did not say that the act occurs by the servant's will; rather He reported that uprightness is attained when the servant wills. We agree with that." And if the Qadari says, "His saying ﴿And you do not will except that God wills﴾ is to be understood as: the servant's will is what necessitates the act by which it occurs, and God's will for the act is His command to do so. We do not deny that."

The answer is that both groups have distorted the text. As for the determinist, it is said to him: according to you, the concomitance of the act with the servant's will is like its concomitance with his existence, his form, and all his other purposes, which have no influence on the act. For according to you, the relation of all his purposes to the act, in terms of having no influence, is a relation of will, and the concomitance is present with all his purposes. So what made the will specifically distinct, in the innate nature, the minds, or the laws of people, between the relation of will and volition to the act and the relation of all the other purposes of the living being, if according to you it is nothing but a customary concomitance? And customary concomitance is present with all of them.

As for the Qadari, his distortion is more severe, because he interpreted "will" as "command." He said that the meaning is: "You do not will except by God's command." This is decisively false, for "will" in the Qur'an is not used in that sense. It is used in the sense of the will of creative decree (*mashīʾat al-takwīn*), as in His saying, ﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾, and His saying, ﴿Had God willed, they would not have fought one another﴾, and His saying, ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾, and His saying, ﴿Have those who believe not despaired that had God willed, He would have guided all of mankind?﴾ and similar passages in which it is impossible to interpret the will as command in any way.

What the verse indicates, together with the other proofs of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) and the clear proofs of reason, is that the wills of the servants are among the existing things that do not come into being except by the will of God, may He be exalted. Whatever He does not will never occurs, just as whatever He wills necessarily occurs.

However, there is a matter here that must be pointed out. God's will, may He be exalted, sometimes relates to His own act and sometimes relates to the act of the servant. Its relation to His own act is that He wills from Himself to assist His servant, grant him success, and prepare him for the act. This will necessitates the servant's act and his will. The will of God for His servant's will alone does not suffice for the occurrence of the act unless He also wills the act itself. For He may will from His servant the will alone, so the servant wills the act and desires it, but does not perform it, because God did not will from Himself to assist him in it and grant him success in it.

This is indicated by His saying, ﴿And you do not will except that God, Lord of the worlds, wills﴾ and His saying, ﴿And they do not remember except that God wills﴾.

These two verses contain the affirmation of the law, the divine decree, the causes and their effects, the act of the servant, and its ascription to the act of the Lord. Each of them has a particular servanthood. The servanthood of the first verse is striving, exhausting one's capacity, free choice, and effort. The servanthood of the second is seeking help from God, relying upon Him, turning to Him, seeking success and aid from Him, and knowing that the servant cannot will or act until God makes him so.

His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ encompasses all of this and contains it. Whoever nullifies either of the two matters has denied the perfection of Lordship (*rubūbiyya*) and nullified it. And success is from God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 81, verses 15–21 (part 1 of 2):

God, glory be to Him, praised His servant Jibril (Gabriel) in the Qur'an in the finest manner, and described him with the most beautiful attributes, saying:
﴿So I swear by the receding stars, (15) the stars that run and hide, (16) and by the night when it retreats, (17) and by the dawn when it breathes, (18) that this is the word of a noble messenger, (19) possessing power, with standing before the Lord of the Throne, (20) obeyed there and trustworthy. (21)﴾
This is Jibril. He described him as God's messenger, as noble in God's sight, as possessing power and a high rank with his Lord, glory be to Him, as obeyed in the heavens, and as trustworthy with the revelation.

As for his nobility before his Lord, he is the closest of the angels to Him.
Some of the early generations (salaf) said: his station with his Lord is like the station of the chamberlain with the king.

As for his power, he lifted up the cities of the people of Lot on his wing, then overturned them upon them.
He is strong in carrying out what he is commanded, unable to fail in it, since the angels of the heavens obey him in what he commands them on behalf of God, exalted is He.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said in his tafsir (exegesis), on the authority of Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Salih: "trustworthy in that he enters seventy pavilions of light without permission."

Describing him as trustworthy requires his truthfulness, his sincerity, and his conveying to the messengers what he was commanded, without addition, subtraction, or concealment.

So the verse combines station, trustworthiness, power, and nearness to God.

A parallel to the combining of station and trustworthiness in him is the words of the Governor to Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us, established and trusted.﴾ [Yusuf: 54]
The combining of power and trustworthiness is like the words of the daughter of Shu'ayb about Musa, peace be upon them both: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy.﴾ [al-Qasas: 26]

(Section)
He said in al-Tibyan:
Among this is God's saying, glory be to Him: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the stars that run and hide﴾
He swore by the stars in their three states: their rising, their running, and their setting.
This is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and the majority of exegetes, and it is the correct one.

Al-khunus is the plural of khanis, and khunus means withdrawing and hiding. From it the devil is called khannas, because he withdraws and shrinks when the servant remembers his Lord. From it is the saying of Abu Hurayrah: "So he withdrew (fa-nkhanasa)." Al-kunus is the plural of kanis, meaning one who enters its kunas, that is, its lair or home. From it: the woman "tkannasat" when she entered her litter, and from it: "the gazelles kanasat" when they took refuge in their lairs.

Al-jawari means the plural of jariyah, like ghashiyah and ghawash. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: "The stars withdraw by day and appear by night." This is also the view of Muqatil, Ata', Qatadah, and others, who said: the planets hide by day, so they are concealed and not seen, and they disappear at the time of their setting. The meaning of "they withdraw" in this view is that they recede from sight and are hidden from it by the daylight covering them. There is another view, that their khunus is their return, and this is their eastward motion, for they have two motions: a motion caused by their own action and a motion by their own nature. Their khunus is their backward motion by their own nature. On this view, the oath is by a type of star, namely the wandering stars (planets).
This is the view of al-Farra'.
There is a third view, that their khunus and kunus is their hiding at the time of their setting, so they set in the places where they set.
This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Since the stars have a state of appearing, a state of hiding, a state of running, and a state of setting, God, glory be to Him, swore by them in all their states. By mentioning their khunus He indicated their state of appearing, because khunus is hiding after appearing, and one does not say of what is still hidden that it has withdrawn. He explicitly mentioned their running and their setting, and their khunus and their appearing. He was content with mentioning their rising by their running, whose beginning is the rising, for rising is the first of their running.
Thus the oath includes their rising, their setting, their running, their hiding, and that is among His signs and proofs of His lordship.

The view of those who explained them as gazelles and wild cattle is not apparent, for several reasons:
First, these states in the wandering stars are a greater sign and lesson.
Second, the people of the earth share in knowing them through observation and sight.
Third, cattle and gazelles have no state in which they are hidden from sight entirely; rather, they are always visible in the open plains.
Fourth, those who explained the verse this way said that their khunus is not from hiding.
Al-Wahidi said: it is from khans in the nose, which is the recession of the nose-tip and the shortness of the bridge; cattle and gazelles have recessed noses, a cow is khansa', and a gazelle is akhnas.
From this the name al-Khansa' derives, from the recession of her nose. It is known that this is a hidden matter that requires reflection, and most people do not know it, whereas the signs of the Lord by which He swears are only apparent and clear, shared in knowledge by all creatures.
The recession in the nose of a cow or gazelle is no greater than the evenness and balance of the nose of the son of Adam, so the sign in the latter is more evident.
Fifth, their kunus in their lairs is no greater than the entry of birds and all other animals into their homes where they shelter, nor is it more evident, so as to be singled out for the oath.
Sixth, if it were the plural of gazelle, it would be said "khans" with a sukun, since it is the plural of akhnas, so it is like ahmar and humr. If it were meant as the plural of a khansa' cow, it would also be on the pattern fa'la', like hamra' and humr. But since its plural came on the pattern fu'al with doubling, it is impossible for it to be the plural of one of the gazelles or cattle, and it is necessarily the plural of khanis, like shahid and shuhud, sa'im and sawm, qa'im and qawm, and their like.
Seventh, it is not clearly acceptable for the Lord, exalted is He, to swear by cattle and gazelles, and this is not the usage or custom of the Qur'an. Rather, God, glory be to Him, swears by the best of each kind, just as when He swore by souls, He swore by the best of them, which is the human soul.
When He swore by His speech, He swore by its noblest and greatest, which is the Qur'an. When He swore by the heavenly things, He swore by the best of them, which are the sky and its sun, moon, and stars.
When He swore by time, He swore by its noblest, which is the ten nights. When He wanted to swear by other than these, He included it in a general term, as in His saying: ﴿So I swear by what you see and what you do not see﴾ and His saying: ﴿the male and the female﴾ in the recitation of the Messenger of God, and similar cases.
Eighth, the conjunction of the oath with the night and the dawn indicates that they are the stars; otherwise it would not be fitting to conjoin cattle and gazelles with night and dawn in one oath.
Abu Ishaq based his argument on this, that they are the stars, saying: this is more fitting to the mention of the stars than to the mention of wild animals.
Ninth, if God had intended that, He would have clarified it and mentioned what indicates it, just as when He intended by the "jawari" the ships, He said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains.﴾
But here there is nothing in the wording or the context indicating that they are cattle and gazelles, while there is in it what indicates that they are the stars, for the reasons we have mentioned and others.
Tenth, the connection between the stars, which are guidance for the travelers and missiles against the devils, and the thing sworn to, which is the Qur'an, which is guidance for the worlds, an adornment for hearts, and a refutation of the devil's doubts, is greater than the connection between cattle, gazelles, and the Qur'an. And God knows best.

(Section)
There is disagreement over the "'as'asa" (approach or departure) of the night: is it its coming or its going? Most scholars hold that 'as'asa means it turned away and departed. This is the view of Ali and Ibn Abbas and his companions.
Al-Hasan said: it came with its darkness, which is one of the two reports from Mujahid.
Whoever favors the coming said: God swore by the coming of the night and the coming of the day, so His saying ﴿and the dawn when it breathes﴾ corresponds to ﴿the night when it retreats﴾.
They said: for this reason God swore by ﴿the night when it covers and the day when it appears﴾ and by the forenoon.
They said: the covering of the night is like its retreat, and the appearing of the day is like the breathing of the dawn, since it is its beginning and its first part.
Whoever favors that it is its departure relies on His saying: ﴿No indeed! By the moon, and by the night when it turns its back, and by the dawn when it brightens﴾, so He swore by the night's departure and the dawn's brightening, which is like the night's retreat and the dawn's breathing.
They said: the better view is that the oath is by the ending of the night and the coming of the day, since it follows it without interval. This is greater in indication and lesson, unlike the coming of the night and the coming of the day, for the oath is not known in the Qur'an by these two. Moreover, there is a long time between them, so the sign in the ending of the one and the arrival of the other immediately after it, without interval, is more eloquent.
So He mentioned the state of this one's weakness and departure, and the state of the other's strength and breathing and approach, which drives away the darkness of the night by its breath. Whenever it breathes, the night flees and turns its back before it. This is the view, and God knows best.

(Section)
Then God, glory be to Him, mentioned the thing sworn to, which is the Qur'an, and informed that it is the word of a noble messenger. Here it is Jibril with certainty, because He described him afterward with what identifies him. As for the noble messenger in al-Haqqah, he is Muhammad, because after it He denied that it is the word of one whom his enemies claimed to be its author. He said: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect.﴾
So He attributed it to the angelic messenger at one time, and to the human messenger at another time. His attribution to each of the two messengers is an attribution of conveying, not of originating it from himself.
Otherwise the two attributions would contradict one another. The word "messenger" indicates this, for the messenger is one who conveys the speech of the one who sent him. This is explicit that it is the speech of the One who sent Jibril and Muhammad, and that each of them conveyed it from God. So it is his word as conveyer, and the word of God, which He spoke truly. There is no ease for one who denies that God speaks the Qur'an, which is His speech in truth, in these two verses. Indeed they are among the clearest proofs that it is the speech of the Lord, exalted is He, and that the two noble messengers have nothing of it except conveying. Jibril heard it from God, and Muhammad heard it from Jibril.

He described his angelic messenger in this surah as noble, strong, established, obeyed in the heavens, and trustworthy with God, the Lord of the Throne. These are five attributes that include the affirmation of the chain of the Qur'an: that it is Muhammad's hearing from Jibril, and Jibril's hearing from the Lord of the worlds. How sublime and exalted is this chain, with God Himself, glory be to Him, attesting to it.

The first attribute: the messenger who brought it to Muhammad is noble, not as his enemies say, that the one who brought it is a devil. The devil is wicked, corrupt, base, ugly in appearance, devoid of good; his inside is worse than his outside, and his outside more hideous than his inside, and there is no good in him or with him. He is the furthest thing from nobility.
